claim: Herbicides with novel modes of action are urgently needed to safeguard global agricultural industries against the damaging effects of herbicide-resistant weeds.
source: Herbicides with novel modes of action are urgently needed to safeguard global agricultural industries against the damaging effects of herbicide-resistant weeds.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of agriculture and herbicide resistance, supported by the citation to Hall et al., 2020 in the Introduction.

claim: The first herbicidal inhibitors of lysine biosynthesis were recently developed, providing proof-of-concept for a promising novel herbicide target.
source: We recently developed the first herbicidal inhibitors of lysine biosynthesis, which provided proof-of-concept for a promising novel herbicide target.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the authors' previous work mentioned in the Abstract and detailed in the Introduction.

claim: Herbicidal lysine biosynthesis inhibitors do not act as proherbicides.
source: We previously postulated that these inhibitors may act as proherbicides. Here, we show this is not the case.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that the demethylated analogue HBDTA has lower activity than MBDTA-2.

claim: MBDTA-2 inhibits a second lysine biosynthesis enzyme in addition to DHDPS.
source: We report an additional mode of action of these inhibitors, through their inhibition of a second lysine biosynthesis enzyme, and investigate the molecular determinants of inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing MBDTA-2 inhibits DHDPR enzymes.

claim: Weeds have evolved resistance to 21 out of the 31 herbicide modes of action.
source: Weeds have now evolved resistance to 21 out of the 31 herbicide modes of action, yet there has been a lack of herbicides with new modes of action brought to market over the last 30 years (Duke and Dayan, 2022; Heap, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Duke and Dayan, 2022 and Heap, 2022.

claim: There has been a lack of herbicides with new modes of action brought to market over the last 30 years.
source: Weeds have now evolved resistance to 21 out of the 31 herbicide modes of action, yet there has been a lack of herbicides with new modes of action brought to market over the last 30 years (Duke and Dayan, 2022; Heap, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Duke and Dayan, 2022 and Heap, 2022.

claim: The inhibition of plant lysine biosynthesis has never been explored commercially for herbicide development.
source: Despite the success of targeting amino acid biosynthesis enzymes for the development of herbicides (e.g. glyphosate and chlorsulfuron), the inhibition of plant lysine biosynthesis has never been explored commercially.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical state of herbicide development, presented as established knowledge.

claim: MBDTA-2 targets lysine production by inhibiting dihydrodipicolinate synthase (DHDPS), the enzyme that catalyses the first and rate-limiting step in the pathway.
source: We showed that the most potent of these inhibitors, (Z)-2-(5-(4-methoxybenzylidene)-2,4-dioxothiazolidin-3-yl)acetic acid (MBDTA-2) (Figure 1A) targets lysine production by inhibiting dihydrodipicolinate synthase (DHDPS), the enzyme that catalyses the first and rate-limiting step in the pathway (Soares da Costa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Soares da Costa et al., 2018.

claim: MBDTA-2 inhibits DHDPS through binding at a novel allosteric site distinct from the allosteric lysine-binding site.
source: Interestingly, we found that the mode of DHDPS inhibition by MBDTA-2 was through binding at a novel allosteric site distinct from the allosteric lysine-binding site (Figure 1B), which enables regulation of the enzyme (Hall et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hall et al., 2021 and Figure 1B showing the binding site.

claim: The in vitro potency of MBDTA-2 against recombinant Arabidopsis thaliana DHDPS enzymes was similar to the activity against agar-grown A. thaliana.
source: In the previous study, we revealed that the in vitro potency of MBDTA-2 against recombinant Arabidopsis thaliana (At) DHDPS enzymes was similar to the activity against agar-grown A. thaliana (Soares da Costa et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Soares da Costa et al., 2021.

claim: Usually, herbicides inhibit their enzyme targets with greater potency than they inhibit in vivo plant growth.
source: Usually, herbicides inhibit their enzyme targets with greater potency than they inhibit in vivo plant growth.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about herbicide behavior.

claim: The amount of herbicide reaching the target site is less than the amount applied.
source: This is because the amount of herbicide reaching the target site is less than the amount applied.
evidence: This is presented as an explanation based on established knowledge of herbicide distribution.

claim: MBDTA-2 could not undergo ester hydrolysis as it does not contain an ester.
source: Whilst MBDTA-2 could not undergo the same process as it does not contain an ester, we postulated that a similar proherbicidal effect may be observed through the in vivo demethylation of the aryl methyl ether.
evidence: This is based on the chemical structure of MBDTA-2.

claim: HBDTA has an IC50 of 100 ± 0.95 µM against AtDHDPS1.
source: The dose–response curves yielded IC50 values for AtDHDPS1 and AtDHDPS2 of 100 ± 0.95 and 105 ± 1.04 µM, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental dose-response data shown in Figure 2.

claim: HBDTA has an IC50 of 105 ± 1.04 µM against AtDHDPS2.
source: The dose–response curves yielded IC50 values for AtDHDPS1 and AtDHDPS2 of 100 ± 0.95 and 105 ± 1.04 µM, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental dose-response data shown in Figure 2.

claim: MBDTA-2 has an IC50 of 63.3 ± 1.80 µM against AtDHDPS1.
source: These values are slightly greater than those we reported for MBDTA-2 (IC50 (AtDHDPS1) = 63.3 ± 1.80 µM, IC50 (AtDHDPS2) = 64.0 ± 1.00 µM) (Soares da Costa et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Soares da Costa et al., 2021.

claim: MBDTA-2 has an IC50 of 64.0 ± 1.00 µM against AtDHDPS2.
source: These values are slightly greater than those we reported for MBDTA-2 (IC50 (AtDHDPS1) = 63.3 ± 1.80 µM, IC50 (AtDHDPS2) = 64.0 ± 1.00 µM) (Soares da Costa et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Soares da Costa et al., 2021.

claim: The activity of MBDTA-2 at the target site is not influenced by the retention or loss of the methyl group in vivo.
source: These data suggest, conversely to our hypothesis, that the activity of MBDTA-2 at the target site is not influenced by the retention or loss of the methyl group in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of IC50 values of HBDTA and MBDTA-2.

claim: Proteins catalysing sequential reactions within a metabolic pathway often have conserved binding site features.
source: It is well established that proteins catalysing sequential reactions within a metabolic pathway often have conserved binding site features (Hsu et al., 2013; Jensen, 1976; Jenwitheesuk et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: MBDTA-2 has an IC50 of 6.92 ± 0.92 µM against AtDHDPR1.
source: The activity of both recombinant A. thaliana DHDPR enzymes was measured whilst titrating MBDTA-2 to determine the IC50 values of 6.92 ± 0.92 µM against AtDHDPR1 and 8.58 ± 1.19 µM against AtDHDPR2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental dose-response data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MBDTA-2 has an IC50 of 8.58 ± 1.19 µM against AtDHDPR2.
source: The activity of both recombinant A. thaliana DHDPR enzymes was measured whilst titrating MBDTA-2 to determine the IC50 values of 6.92 ± 0.92 µM against AtDHDPR1 and 8.58 ± 1.19 µM against AtDHDPR2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental dose-response data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HBDTA has an IC50 of 169 ± 0.92 µM against AtDHDPR1.
source: To do so, we assessed the inhibitory activity of HBDTA against both AtDHDPR isoforms to determine the IC50 values of 169 ± 0.92 and 155 ± 0.90 µM for AtDHDPR1 and AtDHDPR2, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental dose-response data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HBDTA has an IC50 of 155 ± 0.90 µM against AtDHDPR2.
source: To do so, we assessed the inhibitory activity of HBDTA against both AtDHDPR isoforms to determine the IC50 values of 169 ± 0.92 and 155 ± 0.90 µM for AtDHDPR1 and AtDHDPR2, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental dose-response data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HBDTA is >18-fold less potent at the DHDPR target site relative to MBDTA-2.
source: HBDTA is therefore >18-fold less potent at the DHDPR target site relative to MBDTA-2, suggesting that the MBDTA-2 methyl group is beneficial for DHDPR inhibition.
evidence: This is calculated from the IC50 values of HBDTA and MBDTA-2 against DHDPR.

claim: The MBDTA-2 methyl group is beneficial for DHDPR inhibition.
source: HBDTA is therefore >18-fold less potent at the DHDPR target site relative to MBDTA-2, suggesting that the MBDTA-2 methyl group is beneficial for DHDPR inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of IC50 values showing HBDTA (without methyl group) is less potent than MBDTA-2.

claim: MBDTA-2 is unlikely to be a proherbicide.
source: As such, MBDTA-2 is unlikely to be a proherbicide.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the finding that HBDTA is less potent than MBDTA-2 at both target sites.

claim: MBDTA-2 is a multi-targeted inhibitor of two consecutive enzymes in the lysine biosynthesis pathway, AtDHDPS and AtDHDPR.
source: Moreover, these results demonstrate that MBDTA-2 is a multi-targeted inhibitor of two consecutive enzymes in the lysine biosynthesis pathway, AtDHDPS and AtDHDPR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing MBDTA-2 inhibits both AtDHDPS and AtDHDPR.

claim: MBDTA-2 represents the first example of a dual-target inhibitor of the lysine biosynthesis pathway.
source: This compound represents the first example of a dual-target inhibitor of the lysine biosynthesis pathway.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding, based on the experimental data and literature knowledge.

claim: Static docking suggests that MBDTA-2 binds in the AtDHDPR active site with a binding affinity of −6.2 kcal mol−1.
source: The resulting data suggested that MBDTA-2 binds in the active site with a binding affinity of −6.2 kcal mol−1 (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational docking data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The hydrophobic pocket occupied by MBDTA-2 overlaps with the probable NADPH cofactor-binding site.
source: The hydrophobic pocket occupied by MBDTA-2 overlaps with the probable NADPH cofactor-binding site, based on the crystal structure of cofactor-bound Escherichia coli DHDPR (Reddy et al., 1996; Scapin et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on docking results and comparison with E. coli DHDPR crystal structure.

claim: The predicted MBDTA-2 orientation suggests its stabilisation by polar interactions between the heterocyclic ring and Thr122 and Gly120.
source: The predicted MBDTA-2 orientation suggests its stabilisation by polar interactions between the heterocyclic ring and Thr122 and Gly120.
evidence: This is based on the docking model predictions.

claim: The MBDTA-2 acid is within hydrogen bonding proximity to Asp185.
source: Additionally, the MBDTA-2 acid is within hydrogen bonding proximity to Asp185.
evidence: This is based on the docking model predictions.

claim: MBDTA-2 has an IC50 of 72.7 ± 1.07 µM against AtDHDPR1 in the presence of excess substrate and cofactor.
source: The IC50 values determined were 72.7 ± 1.07 and 69.5 ± 1.06 µM for AtDHDPR1 and AtDHDPR2, respectively, which are 10- and 8-fold greater than those determined for AtDHDPR1 and AtDHDPR2 when substrate and cofactor were limiting.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental dose-response data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MBDTA-2 has an IC50 of 69.5 ± 1.06 µM against AtDHDPR2 in the presence of excess substrate and cofactor.
source: The IC50 values determined were 72.7 ± 1.07 and 69.5 ± 1.06 µM for AtDHDPR1 and AtDHDPR2, respectively, which are 10- and 8-fold greater than those determined for AtDHDPR1 and AtDHDPR2 when substrate and cofactor were limiting.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental dose-response data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The IC50 of MBDTA-2 against AtDHDPR1 in the presence of excess substrate and cofactor is 10-fold greater than when substrate and cofactor were limiting.
source: The IC50 values determined were 72.7 ± 1.07 and 69.5 ± 1.06 µM for AtDHDPR1 and AtDHDPR2, respectively, which are 10- and 8-fold greater than those determined for AtDHDPR1 and AtDHDPR2 when substrate and cofactor were limiting.
evidence: This is calculated from comparing IC50 values under different substrate/cofactor conditions.

claim: The IC50 of MBDTA-2 against AtDHDPR2 in the presence of excess substrate and cofactor is 8-fold greater than when substrate and cofactor were limiting.
source: The IC50 values determined were 72.7 ± 1.07 and 69.5 ± 1.06 µM for AtDHDPR1 and AtDHDPR2, respectively, which are 10- and 8-fold greater than those determined for AtDHDPR1 and AtDHDPR2 when substrate and cofactor were limiting.
evidence: This is calculated from comparing IC50 values under different substrate/cofactor conditions.

claim: The apparent reduction in potency of MBDTA-2 in the presence of excess substrate and cofactor indicates that MBDTA-2 is a competitive inhibitor.
source: This apparent reduction in potency indicates that MBDTA-2 is a competitive inhibitor, and therefore likely binds at the AtDHDPR active site as suggested by the docking results.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic behavior showing reduced potency with excess substrate/cofactor.

claim: MBDTA-2 likely binds at the AtDHDPR active site.
source: This apparent reduction in potency indicates that MBDTA-2 is a competitive inhibitor, and therefore likely binds at the AtDHDPR active site as suggested by the docking results.
evidence: This is inferred from the competitive inhibition kinetics and supported by docking results.

claim: The mode of inhibition of MBDTA-2 against AtDHDPR contrasts with the allosteric mode of inhibition of MBDTA-2 against AtDHDPS.
source: Interestingly, this contrasts with the allosteric mode of inhibition of MBDTA-2 against AtDHDPS.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the current findings (competitive inhibition of DHDPR) and previous findings (allosteric inhibition of DHDPS).

claim: MBDTA-2 is the first example of a herbicidal lysine biosynthesis inhibitor.
source: Previously, we showed that the MBDTA-2 compound has herbicidal activity against the model plant A. thaliana and is therefore the first example of a herbicidal lysine biosynthesis inhibitor.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Treatment of L. rigidum with 1200 mg l−1 of MBDTA-2 resulted in inhibition of plant germination and growth.
source: Treatment of L. rigidum with 1200 mg l−1 of MBDTA-2 resulted in inhibition of plant germination and growth, corresponding to a significant reduction in shoot fresh and dry weight and a significant reduction in root dry weight (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Treatment of L. rigidum with 1200 mg l−1 of MBDTA-2 resulted in a significant reduction in shoot fresh and dry weight.
source: Treatment of L. rigidum with 1200 mg l−1 of MBDTA-2 resulted in inhibition of plant germination and growth, corresponding to a significant reduction in shoot fresh and dry weight and a significant reduction in root dry weight (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Treatment of L. rigidum with 1200 mg l−1 of MBDTA-2 resulted in a significant reduction in root dry weight.
source: Treatment of L. rigidum with 1200 mg l−1 of MBDTA-2 resulted in inhibition of plant germination and growth, corresponding to a significant reduction in shoot fresh and dry weight and a significant reduction in root dry weight (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: MBDTA-2 treatment resulted in ~4-fold reduction in shoot fresh weight of L. rigidum.
source: Specifically, we observed ~4- and ~5-fold reductions in shoot fresh and dry weight, respectively, and a ~2-fold reduction in root dry weight (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: MBDTA-2 treatment resulted in ~5-fold reduction in shoot dry weight of L. rigidum.
source: Specifically, we observed ~4- and ~5-fold reductions in shoot fresh and dry weight, respectively, and a ~2-fold reduction in root dry weight (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: MBDTA-2 treatment resulted in ~2-fold reduction in root dry weight of L. rigidum.
source: Specifically, we observed ~4- and ~5-fold reductions in shoot fresh and dry weight, respectively, and a ~2-fold reduction in root dry weight (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The results further exemplify the potential of lysine biosynthesis inhibitors for development as herbicide candidates.
source: These results further exemplify the potential of lysine biosynthesis inhibitors for development as herbicide candidates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results showing herbicidal activity against L. rigidum.

claim: The demethylation of aryl methyl ethers on prodrugs, such as codeine, is well established.
source: While this mechanism of proherbicide conversion has not been reported to date, the demethylation of aryl methyl ethers on prodrugs, such as codeine, is well established (Dayer et al., 1988; Kirchheiner et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dayer et al., 1988 and Kirchheiner et al., 2007.

claim: The mechanism of proherbicide conversion through demethylation of aryl methyl ethers has not been reported to date.
source: While this mechanism of proherbicide conversion has not been reported to date, the demethylation of aryl methyl ethers on prodrugs, such as codeine, is well established (Dayer et al., 1988; Kirchheiner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature regarding proherbicides.

claim: The ~8-fold greater potency of MBDTA-2 against DHDPR than DHDPS reveals that the in vitro potency is actually ~6-fold greater than the in vivo potency.
source: Moreover, the ~8-fold greater potency of MBDTA-2 against DHDPR than DHDPS reveals that the in vitro potency is actually ~6-fold greater than the in vivo potency.
evidence: This is calculated from comparing the IC50 values against DHDPR and DHDPS with in vivo activity.

claim: The low-micromolar potency of MBDTA-2 at the DHDPR target site is comparable to the potency of glyphosate at its enzyme target 5-enolpyruvylshikimate-3-phosphate synthase.
source: Furthermore, the low-micromolar potency of MBDTA-2 at the DHDPR target site is comparable to the potency of glyphosate, the most successful commercial herbicide active ingredient, at its enzyme target 5-enolpyruvylshikimate-3-phosphate synthase (Mao et al., 2016; Sammons et al., 2018).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to Mao et al., 2016 and Sammons et al., 2018.

claim: Glyphosate is the most successful commercial herbicide active ingredient.
source: Furthermore, the low-micromolar potency of MBDTA-2 at the DHDPR target site is comparable to the potency of glyphosate, the most successful commercial herbicide active ingredient, at its enzyme target 5-enolpyruvylshikimate-3-phosphate synthase (Mao et al., 2016; Sammons et al., 2018).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about glyphosate.

claim: The phenomenon of inhibitors having dual-target activity against consecutive enzymes in metabolic pathways has sometimes been attributed to conserved active site features.
source: The phenomenon of inhibitors having dual-target activity against consecutive enzymes in metabolic pathways has sometimes been attributed to conserved active site features (Hsu et al., 2013; Toulouse et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hsu et al., 2013 and Toulouse et al., 2020.

claim: There are many examples of inhibitors of multiple targets from distinct pathways, which have been identified regardless of binding site similarities.
source: However, there are also many examples of inhibitors of multiple targets from distinct pathways, which have been identified regardless of binding site similarities (Allen et al., 2015; Hashmi et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Allen et al., 2015, Hashmi et al., 2021, and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: This is the first time a dual-target inhibitor has been shown to have allosteric and orthosteric inhibitory activity at two different enzymes.
source: Nevertheless, to our knowledge, this is the first time a dual-target inhibitor has been shown to have allosteric and orthosteric inhibitory activity at two different enzymes.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The advantages of multi-target inhibitors over single-target inhibitors have been well reported for the development of novel drugs and fungicides.
source: The advantages of multi-target inhibitors over single-target inhibitors have been well reported for the development of novel drugs and fungicides (Allen et al., 2015; Gullino et al., 2010; Oldfield and Feng, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Allen et al., 2015, Gullino et al., 2010, and Oldfield and Feng, 2014.

claim: A reduced susceptibility to the generation of resistance is a highly desirable property in herbicide development.
source: Such advantages include a reduced susceptibility to the generation of resistance, which is also a highly desirable property in herbicide development (Gressel, 2020; Hall et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gressel, 2020 and Hall et al., 2020.

claim: There has been a focus on the use of herbicide mixtures inhibiting multiple molecular targets in attempts to reduce the generation of resistance to existing herbicides.
source: Indeed, there has been a focus on the use of herbicide mixtures inhibiting multiple molecular targets in attempts to reduce the generation of resistance to existing herbicides (Gressel, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gressel, 2020.

claim: Little work has been done on the development of new herbicides that inhibit multiple targets.
source: Despite the recognition of the potential of inhibiting multiple targets for the reduction of target site resistance generation, little work has been done on the development of new herbicides that do so (Fu et al., 2019; Giberti et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2019 and Giberti et al., 2017.

claim: Dual-target compounds such as MBDTA-2 are promising candidates for progressing the herbicide development field beyond the 'one target-one herbicide' approach.
source: Dual-target compounds such as MBDTA-2 are therefore promising candidates for progressing the herbicide development field beyond the 'one target-one herbicide' approach.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings and literature context.

claim: The previously published DHDPS co-crystal structure and the DHDPR-binding model could be used for the rational design of new MBDTA-2 analogues with increased target site activity.
source: For the future development of dual-target herbicides, the previously published DHDPS co-crystal structure and the DHDPR-binding model presented here could be used for the rational design of new MBDTA-2 analogues with increased target site activity (Soares da Costa et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions based on the current findings.

claim: Formulation has a substantial impact on the performance of herbicide active ingredients.
source: Although these methods offer opportunities to optimise inhibitor potency, formulation also has a substantial impact on the performance of herbicide active ingredients and is therefore an important avenue to pursue for potency maximisation.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about herbicide development.

claim: The development of new herbicides that are effective against L. rigidum is of the highest priority given the economic impact of this species.
source: The development of new herbicides that are effective against L. rigidum, particularly those with a reduced propensity to generate resistance, is of the highest priority given the economic impact of this species.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of L. rigidum as a target for herbicide development.

claim: An overreliance on a small number of herbicide modes of action has culminated in the widespread evolution of multiple resistance mechanisms in L. rigidum.
source: An overreliance on a small number of herbicide modes of action has culminated in the widespread evolution of multiple resistance mechanisms in L. rigidum (Bajwa et al., 2021; Owen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bajwa et al., 2021 and Owen et al., 2014.

claim: In Australia, herbicide-resistant L. rigidum invades 8 million hectares of cropping land.
source: In Australia alone, herbicide-resistant L. rigidum invades 8 million hectares of cropping land, resulting in revenue losses of AUD$93 million annually (Llewellyn et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Llewellyn et al., 2016.

claim: Herbicide-resistant L. rigidum results in revenue losses of AUD$93 million annually in Australia.
source: In Australia alone, herbicide-resistant L. rigidum invades 8 million hectares of cropping land, resulting in revenue losses of AUD$93 million annually (Llewellyn et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Llewellyn et al., 2016.

claim: MBDTA-2 can significantly reduce L. rigidum germination and growth.
source: Our finding that MBDTA-2 can significantly reduce L. rigidum germination and growth further illustrates the potential utility of lysine biosynthesis inhibitors in combatting the global herbicide resistance crisis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing effects on L. rigidum.

claim: The finding that MBDTA-2 can significantly reduce L. rigidum germination and growth illustrates the potential utility of lysine biosynthesis inhibitors in combatting the global herbicide resistance crisis.
source: Our finding that MBDTA-2 can significantly reduce L. rigidum germination and growth further illustrates the potential utility of lysine biosynthesis inhibitors in combatting the global herbicide resistance crisis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings in the context of the herbicide resistance problem.

claim: L. rigidum is one of the most agriculturally problematic weeds in the world.
source: Additionally, we extended our previous in vivo activity studies on A. thaliana to include one of the most agriculturally problematic weeds in the world, rigid ryegrass (Lolium rigidum) (Bajwa et al., 2021; Busi and Beckie, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bajwa et al., 2021 and Busi and Beckie, 2020.

claim: DHDPS catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step in the lysine biosynthesis pathway.
source: We showed that the most potent of these inhibitors, (Z)-2-(5-(4-methoxybenzylidene)-2,4-dioxothiazolidin-3-yl)acetic acid (MBDTA-2) (Figure 1A) targets lysine production by inhibiting dihydrodipicolinate synthase (DHDPS), the enzyme that catalyses the first and rate-limiting step in the pathway (Soares da Costa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the lysine biosynthesis pathway.

claim: DHDPR is the enzyme following DHDPS in the plant lysine biosynthesis pathway.
source: As such, we hypothesised that DHDPS inhibitors may also have activity against the enzyme following DHDPS in the plant lysine biosynthesis pathway, DHDPR.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the lysine biosynthesis pathway.
